paragraphs: It is sometimes asked, with an air of seeming triumph, what inducements the States could have, if disunited, to make war on each other. It would be a full answer to this question to say: precisely the same inducements that have at different times drenched all the nations of the world in blood. But, unfortunately for us, the question admits of a more particular answer. There are causes of difference within our immediate view, and we have had enough experience of their tendency, even under the restraints of a federal constitution, to form a judgment of what might be expected if those restraints were removed.

Territorial disputes have at all times been found one of the most fertile sources of hostility among nations. Perhaps the greatest proportion of the wars that have desolated the earth have sprung from this origin. This cause would exist among us in full force. We have a vast tract of unsettled territory within the boundaries of the United States. There are still discordant and undecided claims between several of the States, and the dissolution of the Union would lay a foundation for similar claims between them all. It is well known that they have heretofore had serious and heated discussion about the rights to the lands that were ungranted at the time of the Revolution and that usually went by the name of crown lands. The States within the limits of whose colonial governments those lands lay have claimed them as their property. The others have contended that the rights of the crown in this matter passed to the Union, especially as to all that part of the Western territory which, whether by actual possession or through the submission of the Indian proprietors, was subject to the jurisdiction of the king of Great Britain until he gave it up in the treaty of peace. This, it has been said, was in any event an acquisition to the Confederacy by compact with a foreign power. It has been the prudent policy of Congress to appease this controversy by prevailing on the States to make cessions to the United States for the benefit of the whole. This has been accomplished far enough to give, if the Union continues, a decided prospect of a friendly end to the dispute. A breakup of the Confederacy, however, would revive this dispute and would create others on the same subject. At present a large part of the vacant Western territory is, by cession at least, if not by any earlier right, the common property of the Union. If the Union were at an end, the States that made the cession, on a principle of federal compromise, would be apt to reclaim the lands as a reversion once the motive for the grant had ceased. The other States would no doubt insist on a proportion, by right of representation. Their argument would be that a grant, once made, could not be revoked, and that the justice of sharing in territory acquired or secured by the joint efforts of the Confederacy remained undiminished. If, contrary to probability, all the States should admit that each had a right to a share of this common stock, there would still be a difficulty to overcome in finding a proper rule of apportionment. Different States would set up different principles for this purpose, and as these would affect the opposite interests of the parties, they might not easily be open to a peaceful settlement.

In the wide field of Western territory, therefore, we see an ample theater for hostile claims, with no umpire or common judge to step between the contending parties. Reasoning from the past to the future, we shall have good ground to fear that the sword would sometimes be appealed to as the arbiter of their differences. The circumstances of the dispute between Connecticut and Pennsylvania over the land at Wyoming warn us not to be sanguine in expecting an easy settlement of such differences. The articles of confederation obliged the parties to submit the matter to the decision of a federal court. The submission was made, and the court decided in favor of Pennsylvania. But Connecticut gave strong signs of dissatisfaction with that decision, and she did not appear to be entirely resigned to it until, by negotiation and management, something like an equivalent was found for the loss she supposed herself to have suffered. Nothing said here is intended to convey the slightest censure of the conduct of that State. She no doubt sincerely believed herself to have been injured by the decision, and States, like individuals, accept decisions to their disadvantage with great reluctance.

Those who had an opportunity to see the inside of the transactions that accompanied the progress of the controversy between this State and the district of Vermont can vouch for the opposition we experienced, from States not concerned as well as from those that were concerned in the claim. They can attest the danger to which the peace of the Confederacy might have been exposed had this State attempted to assert its rights by force. Two motives preponderated in that opposition. One was a jealousy of our future power, and the other was the interest of certain influential individuals in the neighboring States who had obtained grants of lands under the actual government of that district. Even the States that brought forward claims contradicting ours seemed more anxious to dismember this State than to establish their own pretensions. These were New Hampshire, Massachusetts, and Connecticut. New Jersey and Rhode Island, on all occasions, showed a warm zeal for the independence of Vermont, and Maryland entered deeply into the same views until she was alarmed by the appearance of a connection between Canada and that State. These being small States, they looked with an unfriendly eye on the prospect of our growing greatness. In a review of these transactions we may trace some of the causes that would be likely to embroil the States with each other if it should be their unfortunate destiny to become disunited.

The competitions of commerce would be another fruitful source of contention. The States less favorably situated would wish to escape the disadvantages of their location and to share in the advantages of their more fortunate neighbors. Each State, or separate confederacy, would pursue a system of commercial policy peculiar to itself. This would cause distinctions, preferences, and exclusions, which would breed discontent. The habits of intercourse on the basis of equal privileges, to which we have been accustomed since the earliest settlement of the country, would give a keener edge to those causes of discontent than they would naturally have without this circumstance. WE SHOULD BE READY TO CALL INJURIES THOSE THINGS WHICH WERE IN REALITY THE JUSTIFIABLE ACTS OF INDEPENDENT SOVEREIGNTIES CONSULTING A DISTINCT INTEREST. The spirit of enterprise that characterizes the commercial part of America has left no occasion for displaying itself unused. It is not at all probable that this unbridled spirit would pay much respect to those regulations of trade by which particular States might try to secure exclusive benefits for their own citizens. The violations of these regulations on one side, and the efforts to prevent and repel them on the other, would naturally lead to outrages, and these to reprisals and wars.

The opportunities that some States would have of making others tributary to them by commercial regulations would be submitted to impatiently by the tributary States. The relative situation of New York, Connecticut, and New Jersey would offer an example of this kind. New York, from the necessities of revenue, must lay duties on her imports. A great part of these duties must be paid by the inhabitants of the two other States as consumers of what we import. New York would be neither willing nor able to give up this advantage. Her citizens would not consent that a duty paid by them should be remitted in favor of the citizens of her neighbors, nor would it be practicable, even if this obstacle did not stand in the way, to distinguish the customers in our own markets. Would Connecticut and New Jersey long submit to be taxed by New York for her exclusive benefit? Should we be long permitted to remain in the quiet and undisturbed enjoyment of a metropolis, the possession of which gave us an advantage so odious to our neighbors and, in their opinion, so oppressive? Should we be able to keep it against the overhanging weight of Connecticut on the one side and the cooperating pressure of New Jersey on the other? These are questions that only recklessness will answer in the affirmative.

The public debt of the Union would be a further cause of collision between the separate States or confederacies. The apportionment in the first instance, and the gradual paying off afterward, would alike produce ill-humor and animosity. How would it be possible to agree on a rule of apportionment satisfactory to all? There is scarcely any that can be proposed that is entirely free from real objections. These, as usual, would be exaggerated by the opposing interests of the parties. There are even different views among the States about the general principle of paying off the public debt. Some of them, either less impressed with the importance of national credit, or because their citizens have little, if any, immediate interest in the question, feel an indifference, if not a repugnance, to paying the domestic debt at all. These would be inclined to magnify the difficulties of a distribution. Others, in which a numerous body of citizens are creditors of the public out of proportion to the State's share of the total national debt, would be strenuous for some equitable and effective provision. The delays of the former would excite the resentment of the latter. In the meantime, the settlement of a rule would be postponed by real differences of opinion and pretended delays. The citizens of the States concerned would clamor, foreign powers would press for satisfaction of their just demands, and the peace of the States would be exposed to the double risk of external invasion and internal contention.

Suppose the difficulties of agreeing on a rule were overcome and the apportionment made. There would still be great reason to suppose that the rule agreed on would, when tried, be found to bear harder on some States than on others. Those that suffered by it would naturally seek relief from the burden. The others would as naturally be unwilling to revise it, since a revision was likely to end in an increase of their own burdens. Their refusal would be too plausible a pretext for the complaining States to withhold their contributions not to be seized on eagerly, and the failure of these States to meet their engagements would be a ground for bitter discussion and altercation. Even if the rule adopted should in practice bear out the equality of its principle, delinquencies in payments on the part of some of the States would still result from a variety of other causes: a real deficiency of resources, the mismanagement of their finances, accidental disorders in the management of the government, and, in addition to the rest, the reluctance with which men commonly part with money for purposes that have outlived the emergencies that produced them and that interfere with the supply of immediate wants. Delinquencies, from whatever causes, would produce complaints, recriminations, and quarrels. There is, perhaps, nothing more likely to disturb the tranquillity of nations than their being bound to mutual contributions for any common object that does not yield an equal and simultaneous benefit. For it is an observation as true as it is trite that there is nothing men differ about so readily as the payment of money.

Laws in violation of private contracts, since they amount to aggressions on the rights of those States whose citizens are injured by them, may be considered another probable source of hostility. We are not entitled to expect that a more liberal or more equitable spirit would preside over the legislation of the individual States hereafter, if unrestrained by any additional checks, than we have heretofore seen, in too many instances, disgracing their separate codes. We have observed the disposition to retaliate that was excited in Connecticut by the outrages committed by the Legislature of Rhode Island, and we reasonably infer that in similar cases, under other circumstances, a war, not of PARCHMENT but of the sword, would punish such atrocious breaches of moral obligation and social justice.

The probability of incompatible alliances between the different States or confederacies and different foreign nations, and the effects of this situation on the peace of the whole, have been sufficiently set out in some preceding papers. From the view they have given of this part of the subject, this conclusion is to be drawn: that America, if not connected at all, or connected only by the feeble tie of a simple league, offensive and defensive, would, by the working of such clashing alliances, be gradually entangled in all the destructive labyrinths of European politics and wars. By the destructive contentions of the parts into which she was divided, she would be likely to become a prey to the artifices and machinations of powers equally the enemies of them all. Divide et impera(1) must be the motto of every nation that either hates or fears us.(2)

2. In order that the whole subject of these papers may as soon as possible be laid before the public, it is proposed to publish them four times a week—on Tuesday in the New York Packet and on Thursday in the Daily Advertiser.
